sourceBindings.text: A field-sampling section may be called Methods, Methodology or Field Sampling Procedures. Its purpose is reproducibility: another competent person should understand the procedure well enough to repeat it under stated conditions. It is not written to reach a page count, justify a budget or praise the field team.

Follow the information chain: observe the field, record the context, collect and identify the sample, maintain its handling record, receive the laboratory result and interpret them together. Missing field records, with no trustworthy traceable equivalent, or an unmatched sample ID break a link. A precise laboratory number cannot reconstruct undocumented field conditions.

Write concise, objective sentences. Describe what actually happened and any deviation. A formal tone does not require hiding uncertainty. 'Sampling time was not recorded' is more defensible than inventing a plausible time to make a paragraph look complete.

Prepare three connected items: a durable labeled container, a field sheet and a method paragraph. They have different jobs, but the sample identity, location, date/time, method and handling must agree wherever repeated.

Preserve all negations, conditions, scene-safety restrictions and limits of training. Do not add medical advice, diagnoses, character voices, an introduction, music or an extra summary.

sourceBindings.text: First state the objective and design: why the sample was collected and how locations were chosen. A grid, randomized locations and selected topographic features are different designs. Name the one actually used. Do not call a convenient route random unless locations were chosen by a defined random method.

Next state the collection procedure: preparation of the location, clean tool, sampled layer and quantity where recorded. Clearing surface litter is different from stripping away the soil layer you intend to test. Record depth with units and enough detail to identify the sampled interval.

Finally state sample handling: approved container, identification, preservation checks, custody and transport. Quote only conditions established by the record or supplied scenario. A cooler is not proof of a measured temperature; a deadline is not proof of an actual arrival time.

Highlight the why, where/how, tool, depth, label and storage in a model paragraph. Then check each highlighted statement against the field sheet. This is a practical way to detect a polished sentence that has no supporting record.

sourceBindings.text: The Greenfield Farm example uses five separate sampling locations in North Paddock: one on the crest, two on the middle slope and two in the low-lying area. Its stated purpose is baseline nutrient information, and its collection date is 26 October 2024. The topographic choices describe this example; they are not a replacement for the earlier ten-point composite-sampling task.

The example uses a cleaned stainless steel hand auger and the 0–15 cm layer, with approximately 500 g collected at each location. Each location has its own sample identity. Keeping these samples separate preserves the differences the design is intended to compare.

The handling example specifies new sealed polyethylene bags, durable identities and a cooled transfer around 4°C with delivery within six hours. These are supplied scenario conditions. An actual laboratory must confirm container, preservation and timing for the named analysis; they are not universal rules for nutrient tests.

Check the arithmetic and identity: one plus two plus two equals five locations. Do not report one composite if five separate bags were collected, and do not claim ten subsamples because another exercise used ten. Describe the design in front of you.

sourceBindings.text: Use the Riverside Park Expansion scenario, code RPE, at Site 3 – Proposed Playground. It is a flat grassy area. The supplied collection time is 11:00 and the layer is 0–15 cm. The stated purpose is background soil information for heavy-metal analysis. This is a simulated documentation exercise with safe material, not an instruction to investigate a contaminated site.

The supplied appearance is dark brown and slightly sticky. Record those observations as scenario data. The scenario also names clay loam; record that as a supplied classification, not a conclusion proved by colour and slight stickiness alone. If the classification must be established independently, perform the relevant test.

Use the exercise date, explicitly identified as the scenario date, and your own exercise initials. Create the unique ID RPE-S3-01 if it is unused in the practice project. Use the supplied stainless steel trowel and cooled-transfer details as model conditions. Mark missing weather, coordinates or measured temperature 'not supplied' rather than inventing a field observation.

Work in a group of two or three where available, but produce attributable work. Allow about fifteen minutes for labeling and recording, ten for the method paragraph and ten for peer review: thirty-five minutes in all. These are planning times, not automatic pass/fail timers. Online, a shared document or structured review form can support the same exchange.

sourceBindings.text: Exchange the labeled container, field sheet and paragraph with a partner. Check all six label groups, matching IDs, data provenance and whether the report states the objective, tool, depth and handling. A field marked honestly unavailable is different from one silently omitted or filled with a guess.

Give specific feedback: 'The bag says RPE-S3-01 but the paragraph says RPE-S3-10; check the collection record and correct the mismatch transparently.' Avoid comments such as 'make it better' that do not identify an action. Retain the earlier record and correction history.

If you need support, use a label with preprinted fields and sentence starters: 'On [recorded date], sample [ID] was collected to…'; 'The location and design were…'; 'Using [tool], the layer…'; 'The sample was then…'. Fill only what the evidence supports.

For a challenge, the scenario adds a discoloured patch of grass two metres from the sampling point. Record its position and appearance as a supplied scenario observation and explain why it may merit separate investigation. Do not diagnose contamination or silently include its soil in the existing sample.

A colleague hands you a bag with only GPS coordinates. Ask for the unique ID and project, the depth and collection method, and the date/time and handling history. Coordinates alone cannot establish what the sample represents or whether the preservation requirement was met.
